barriers.description: Target users were unfamiliar with the novel concept of content-based visual search, making it hard for designers to introduce and validate the approach with users.
barriers.justification: Users' inability to readily adopt the content-based search concept hindered the designers' work to manage user understanding and to facilitate meaningful user involvement and feedback during early requirement elicitation.
barriers.reference_excerpt: We learned that for all users the general idea was inspiring. Still, it was difficult for them to adapt the concept of searching in the data content, since this possibility was not given before.

barriers.description: A 'chicken-and-egg' dilemma existed: developers needed well-defined user requirements to build prototypes, while users needed prototypes or visual inspiration to articulate requirements.
barriers.justification: This mutual dependency explicitly impeded the designers' ability to specify user requirements and plan effective iterative prototyping cycles, constraining the process of producing and validating design solutions.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Be aware of this classical “chicken-and-egg” dilemma originating from knowledge gaps between different stakeholders [52]: on one hand, it is difficult for the computer scientist to provide a prototype without well-defined user requirements derived from domain knowledge. On the other hand, users will have difficulties in defining requirements without any visual inspiration derived from expertise in visualization designs.

barriers.description: Scientists expressed limited trust in third-party data and questioned the precision of overview visualizations, preferring data from trusted colleagues.
barriers.justification: This trust and precision concern limited designers' ability to facilitate user involvement and to address the holistic user experience, forcing them to invest additional effort into data curation and tightly integrated detail-on-demand to gain users' acceptance.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Many scientists prefer to analyze primarily their own data, or data they receive from colleague scientists they trust. Moreover, using advanced visualization capability was seen in a bipolar way by some scientists. On the one hand, it was recognized that visual overviews can greatly enhance screening and comparison tasks. On the other hand, scientists were questioning the precision of the visual representations of the data.

barriers.description: Users had varied and uncertain notions of time-series similarity, wanting many alternative similarity definitions, while designers feared overloading the system with too many parameters.
barriers.justification: This tension constrained the designers' ability to specify stable user requirements and to produce design solutions that balance flexibility and usability, complicating the definition of actionable similarity options and iteration strategies.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Still, we learned that scientists are often not entirely sure about how to formally define the perspective similarity for their search. As scientists pointed out, they ideally want to have many different similarity definitions at hand, and compare the search results they obtain, to decide upon the most appropriate similarity function. Yet our assumption is that overloading the search system with too many parameters (e.g., similarity search parameters) would detriment the usability and make the learning process more complicated.

barriers.description: Early stages of the project lacked a sufficiently integrative focus on usability, and the team recognized that earlier usability assessment would have been desirable.
barriers.justification: The absence of early, embedded usability attention hindered the designers' ability to manage user familiarization, to integrate feedback early, and to iteratively evaluate prototypes efficiently, increasing learning costs for users and rework for designers.
barriers.reference_excerpt: One of the lessons learned is that the usability of the system needs to be well grounded. Looking back, an even more integrative approach, especially in the early design stages, would have been desirable. A lesson learned for future projects is to make early assessment of usability aspects mandatory.

barriers.description: Early prototype interaction and interface design features (e.g., Visual Catalog colormap, loading cell patterns into the Sketch Editor, sketching interaction, and facet design) were confusing to users and impeded task completion.
barriers.justification: These concrete usability failings constrained designers' ability to evaluate and iterate effectively because participants struggled to perform core tasks, reducing the quality of feedback and necessitating substantial redesign work to support evaluation and iteration workloads.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Task 1 uncovered problems regarding the interface of the Visual Catalog. The applied colormap concept caused confusion since it was an unknown term for 10 participants (53%). Therefore, the colormap was removed in the following implementation phase. In task 2, most severities dealt with the problem that users were unsure how to use a cell pattern of the Visual Catalog as an example query and how it could be loaded into the Sketch Editor. With this version of the Sketch Editor, the users were unsure how to draw a curve pattern. Task 4 revealed that the concept of faceting was new to many users. It became clear that the facet design was not intuitive.
